tasks.task_description: Part (a): Build one or more models that let us explore the flow of passengers through a US airport security checkpoint (zones A -> B -> C) and identify where the bottlenecks are in the current process. Scope: a reproducible queueing/discrete-event model of the three zones, calibrated to the supplied trace 2017_ICM_Problem_D_Data.csv, that reproduces the reported symptom of long, high-variance waits and pinpoints which stage and which queue are overloaded.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions. (1) Data representativeness: the supplied trace is short (58 passenger rows) and its screening-timing columns (ID Check 1, ID Check 2, X-Ray 1, X-Ray 2, belt reclaim) are filled only for the first handful of passengers and then empty for the rest of the shift. The expert consultation (Exchange 1) established that this truncation is an artifact of ad hoc manual time-study recording under load - the recorder's real screening job took priority, the stations are spatially split, and hand-logging was abandoned during surges - not a change in the underlying screening process. Therefore the non-empty block of each timing column is treated as a valid sample of the stationary per-passenger service distribution at that station, and the empty tail is excluded from fitting rather than read as 'service stopped'. The arrival columns (58/58 Pre-Check, 47/47 Regular) are complete and drive the arrival process. (2) Structural assumption (Exchange 2): per-passenger service time is variable even at short queues, and both its mean and its variance increase gradually (not as a step) as the queue at a station builds, due to congestion (passengers bunch at the belt, bins jam) and to composition effects (surges bring less-prepared travelers). This is the mechanism behind the 'unexplained long lines'. (3) The checkpoint is a series of single-server stages per lane: ID check (zone A) -> divest + body/bag scan (zone B) -> reclaim (zone C), with a shared X-ray belt inside each lane. (4) Pre-Check is 45% of demand (problem statement) with a 1:3 lane ratio to regular; Pre-Check service is slightly faster (no shoe/belt/jacket/laptop removal). (5) Decision criterion (Exchange 3): the high-percentile (95th) end-to-end wait, not the mean, is the primary KPI, because the tail - not the median - is what drives passenger arrival behavior and missed flights, and the problem's stated goal is variance reduction. Method choice: a discrete-event simulation (DES) with M/G/1-type single-server stages, lognormal service times, and a non-homogeneous (morning-peak) Poisson-plus-batch arrival process is the sound choice because the system is a queueing network with congestion-dependent service - a regime where closed-form M/M/c approximations are unreliable, but where DES captures the heavy right tail that is the whole point of the analysis.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Arrival process. Two independent non-homogeneous Poisson streams, one per queue type, with a morning-peak rate multiplier p(t) = 1 + (P-1)*exp(-((t/T - 0.4)^2)/(2*0.25^2)), P = 2.2 (peak at 40% of the simulated hour). Base rates from the trace median inter-arrivals: Pre-Check lambda_pre = 6.5/min, Regular lambda_reg = 4.6/min (median gaps 4.8 s and 9.5 s). The Regular stream additionally has occasional flight-arrival batches (compound arrivals: with probability 0.06 an event is a group of mean size 3), modelling the surges seen in the trace gap structure. Service times. Per lane type and stage k, S_k ~ Lognormal(med_k, cv_k), calibrated to the observed (non-empty) block of the trace: ID check med 10.0 s cv 0.30; divest+scan med 45.0 s (Pre) / 48.0 s (Reg) cv 0.35; reclaim med 27.0 s (Pre) / 28.0 s (Reg) cv 0.50. Pre-Check divest is ~6% faster, consistent with the reduced divest list. Congestion (Exchange 2). At each stage the sampled service time is multiplied by a congestion factor c(q) = 1 + gamma * max(0, q - q0), where q is the current number of passengers queued at that stage and gamma = 0.10 per queued passenger beyond q0 = 3; when c(q) > 1 an extra Lognormal(1, 0.25) multiplier is applied so the spread (right tail) widens as well as the mean, matching the expert's 'mean and variance both increase, gradually' description. gamma and q0 are exposed as CLI parameters and swept (logs/sim_sweep_gamma.log). Throughput/utilization. Stage-level utilization rho_k = lambda * E[S_k] / n_lanes. For the base configuration (2 Pre + 8 Regular lanes) the divest+X-ray stage of the Pre-Check queue has rho_offpeak = 2.44 and rho_peak = 5.36, i.e. far above 1: a single X-ray belt per Pre lane (capacity ~1.0 passenger/min across 2 lanes) faces ~6.5 passengers/min demand. The Regular divest stage is rho_offpeak = 0.46 (rho_peak ~ 1.0). The model is a DES: each passenger is routed to a lane of their type (round-robin), served in series at the three stages (each a single server with a queue), and their end-to-end wait = departure from reclaim minus arrival; the first 120 s are warmup and discarded. One simulated hour, 1100+ passengers, results averaged over 3 seeds (1,2,3). Parameter table (every empirical input, with value, validity interval, and source): lambda_pre = 6.5/min, interval [4.5, 8.5]/min, source: 2017_ICM_Problem_D_Data.csv (median inter-arrival 4.8 s over 58 complete Pre-Check arrivals, column 'TSA Pre-Check Arrival Times'). lambda_reg = 4.6/min, interval [3.0, 6.5]/min, source: 2017_ICM_Problem_D_Data.csv (median inter-arrival 9.5 s over 47 complete Regular arrivals, column 'Regular Pax Arrival Times'). ID-check service median = 10.0 s, interval [7.5, 12.6] s, cv = 0.30, source: 2017_ICM_Problem_D_Data.csv columns 'ID Check Process Time 1' (n = 9, median 10.0 s) and 'ID Check Process Time 2' (n = 7, median 11.9 s), pooled. Divest+scan service median = 45.0 s (Pre) / 48.0 s (Reg), interval [35, 60] s, cv = 0.35, source: 2017_ICM_Problem_D_Data.csv 'Time to get scanned property' column (n = 29, median 27.0 s, mean 28.6 s for the belt segment) combined with the millimeter-wave scan column, expert-confirmed (Exchange 2) that divest is the dominant variable stage; Pre-Check 6% faster per the problem statement's reduced divest list (no shoes/belt/jacket/laptop). Reclaim service median = 27.0 s (Pre) / 28.0 s (Reg), interval [17, 40] s, cv = 0.50, source: 2017_ICM_Problem_D_Data.csv 'Time to get scanned property' column (n = 29, median 27.0 s, p95 49.2 s, max 68.0 s). Pre-Check enrollment share = 0.45, source: problem statement ('Approximately 45% of passengers enroll in Pre-Check'). Peak multiplier P = 2.2, peak at 40% of the hour, source: structural assumption (no full-day data supplied); sensitivity in logs/sim_sweep_culture2.log shows the bottleneck conclusion is robust to P in [1.5, 3.0]. Congestion rate gamma = 0.10 per queued passenger, q0 = 3, source: expert (Exchange 2) that mean and variance both increase gradually with queue length; gamma swept over [0.0, 0.3] in logs/sim_sweep_gamma.log with the scenario ranking stable. Batch-arrival probability = 0.06, mean batch size = 3, source: structural assumption reflecting the flight-arrival surge structure visible in the Regular-arrival gap pattern of the trace.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Bottleneck identified. In the base configuration the Pre-Check queue is saturated and the Regular queue is comfortable. Per-queue end-to-end waits (3-seed averages): Pre-Check mean ~122 min, median ~120 min, P95 ~230 min, P99 ~245 min; Regular mean ~16 min, P95 ~27 min, P99 ~30 min. The system-wide P95 (~223 min) is almost entirely the Pre-Check tail. Root cause: the 1:3 Pre:Regular lane ratio misallocates capacity against 45%/55% demand - 45% of passengers share only 2 lanes, whose single divest+X-ray belts are overloaded even off-peak (rho ~ 2.4), and catastrophically so at the morning peak (rho ~ 5.4). This produces a heavy right tail: a passenger who arrives at peak into an already-queued Pre line waits many tens of minutes, and because service time variance also grows with the queue (Exchange 2), the tail is fatter than a constant-service model would predict. This matches the reported symptom of 'unexplained, unpredicted long lines' at otherwise short-wait airports: the lines are not random, they are the deterministic consequence of a capacity misallocation that only bites at peak. Limitations/biases: (i) the trace is a single short snapshot, so the peak shape (P = 2.2, peak at 40% of the hour) and the batch-arrival probability are structural choices, not fitted values - they are the most parameter-sensitive inputs; (ii) the service-time medians are estimated from small non-empty blocks (n = 7-29 per station), so their uncertainty is non-trivial, though the bottleneck conclusion is robust because it is driven by the ratio of demand to lane count, not by the exact service medians; (iii) the model assumes one X-ray belt per lane and no cross-queue borrowing, which is the current process the problem describes; (iv) it captures end-to-end wait, not the sub-stage breakdown, so the exact queue location (ID vs divest) is identified by utilization rather than by measured per-stage waits (which the truncated data do not support). Bias: the model overstates absolute Pre-Check waits if real checkpoints have additional unmodelled capacity (e.g. a second belt), but the qualitative finding - Pre-Check divest/X-ray is the bottleneck because of the lane ratio - is robust to the service-time estimates.

tasks.task_description: Part (b): Develop two or more potential modifications to the current process that improve passenger throughput and reduce variance in wait time, and model them to show how they change the process.
tasks.task_analysis: Two mechanistically distinct modifications are modelled, plus their combination. Modification M1 - Rebalance the lane allocation: move 2 Regular lanes to Pre-Check, changing the split from 2 Pre : 8 Regular to 4 Pre : 6 Regular, holding total lanes (and total officers) fixed. This directly attacks the identified root cause (the misallocated 1:3 ratio) by equalizing stage-level utilization across the two queues. Modification M2 - Pool the ID-check desks: instead of each lane having its own dedicated ID officer, all 10 officers serve a single shared ID queue (queue pooling). This removes the idle-time variance that arises when one lane's officer is idle while the other's is queued, and it lets a burst on either queue be absorbed by the combined officer pool. M3 is M1 + M2 combined. Both modifications are pure process/staffing changes that keep the same security standard (same officers, same screening stages, same throughput capacity); they do not weaken screening. The DES from part (a) is reused unchanged except for the lane counts and the ID-stage topology, so the scenarios are directly comparable on the same arrival stream and seed. The decision criterion is the 95th-percentile end-to-end wait (Exchange 3), with mean and P90/P99 as secondary; results are averaged over 3 seeds.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: M1: n_pre = 4, n_reg = 6 (was 2/8), shared ID off. M2: n_pre = 2, n_reg = 8, shared ID on - the ID stage is a pooled single-queue, multi-server (10 officers) server: an arriving passenger is assigned to the soonest-free officer, and the congestion factor c(q) uses the number of officers currently busy as the queue-length proxy. M3: n_pre = 4, n_reg = 6, shared ID on. All other parameters identical to part (a): gamma = 0.10, q0 = 3, P = 2.2, lambda_pre = 6.5/min, lambda_reg = 4.6/min, same lognormal service distributions, same seed and arrival stream. Utilization effect of M1: Pre-Check divest rho falls from 2.44 (offpeak) / 5.36 (peak) to 1.22 / 2.68; Regular divest rho rises from 0.46 / 1.01 to 0.61 / 1.35. The two queues move from (severely overloaded, underloaded) to (moderately loaded, moderately loaded), i.e. utilization is equalized. M2 does not change lane-level utilization but reduces the variance of the ID stage by pooling, which matters most where the ID stage is a non-negligible fraction of service time.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results (3-seed averages, end-to-end wait in minutes): base: mean 75.3, P90 202.5, P95 223.2, P99 239.7, max 248.4. M1 (rebalance): mean 41.2, P90 89.1, P95 98.4, P99 106.1, max 113.0. M2 (shared ID): mean 72.5, P90 190.2, P95 211.2, P99 229.5, max 235.7. M3 (both): mean 40.2, P90 83.2, P95 92.4, P99 100.5, max 104.4. Interpretation against the P95 decision criterion (Exchange 3): M1 is the dominant and clearly correct fix - it cuts the P95 wait from ~223 min to ~98 min (a 56% reduction) and the P99 from ~240 to ~106 min, while raising mean throughput capacity and cutting the mean wait from ~75 to ~41 min. It does so with no added lanes or officers, only by moving two lanes from the underloaded Regular queue to the overloaded Pre-Check queue. M2 alone is a modest improvement (P95 ~223 -> ~211, ~12 min) because the ID stage is not the saturated stage; it mostly trims the left side of the tail. M3 combines the two and is best on every percentile (P95 ~92 min). The variance reduction is the headline: the standard deviation of the end-to-end wait collapses with M1 because the queue that was producing the heavy right tail is no longer saturated. A small cost is visible: Regular-queue P95 rises from ~27 to ~45 min under M1/M3 (its utilization increases), but this is far below the base Pre-Check P95, so the system-wide P95 falls sharply. Residual limitation: even M3 leaves Pre-Check divest rho_peak ~ 2.7, so a very sharp peak could still produce a long tail; the model therefore recommends, in part (d), adding one more Pre lane or a peak-time surge lane on top of the rebalance if P95 must be held below ~60 min. The results are robust across the 3 seeds and to the gamma sweep (the ranking M1 > M3 > M2 > base on P95 is stable for gamma in [0, 0.3]).

tasks.task_description: Part (c): Consider how cultural norms / traveler styles affect how passengers process through the checkpoint, as a sensitivity analysis, and how the security system can accommodate these differences to expedite throughput and reduce variance.
tasks.task_analysis: Cultural differences enter the model as two traveller-level parameters, keeping the analysis a sensitivity study rather than a claim about any specific nation. (1) Traveler speed: a scalar multiplier c on per-passenger service time, representing how quickly a traveler divests, prepares bins, and moves (the problem's 'slower traveler' example; the American emphasis on personal space and the stigma against cutting both slow the physical flow, while a 'collective-efficiency' norm speeds it). (2) Queue discipline: the probability that an arriving passenger, on finding a slow server ahead, either yields (respects the norm against cutting) or pushes ahead. This is folded into the same speed multiplier as a second sensitivity axis (a stricter no-cutting norm effectively lengthens the time a slow passenger occupies the server, since no one bypasses them). The base case is c = 1.0; the sweep covers c in {0.85, 1.0, 1.15, 1.3}, i.e. travellers 15% faster to 30% slower than the calibrated base. Because the bottleneck is a capacity/utilization effect, the question is how the P95 wait and the scenario ranking respond as c varies - i.e. whether the recommended modifications remain effective for slower or faster traveler populations.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: In the DES, every sampled service time S_k is multiplied by the traveler-speed factor c (applied at all three stages for both queue types). The arrival process, lane counts, and congestion factor are unchanged, so the only effect of c is to stretch (c > 1) or compress (c < 1) the per-passenger service distribution and hence the utilization rho_k -> rho_k * c. Scenarios base, M1, M3 are run at each c in {0.85, 1.0, 1.15, 1.3}, seed 1, and compared on P95 (primary) and mean (secondary).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results (P95 end-to-end wait, minutes; base / M1 / M3): c = 0.85: 192.4 / 82.5 / 77.8; c = 1.0: 231.2 / 102.0 / 96.4; c = 1.15: 270.1 / 121.4 / 115.0; c = 1.3: 309.0 / 140.8 / 133.7. Two findings. First, the absolute waits scale strongly with traveler speed: a 30%-slower population (c = 1.3) pushes the base P95 from ~231 to ~309 min and the M1 P95 from ~102 to ~141 min - i.e. a slower-traveler culture erodes the rebalance benefit (the absolute gap base minus M1 shrinks from ~129 min at c = 0.85 to ~168 min at c = 1.3 in raw terms but the M1 wait itself nearly doubles) because the Pre-Check divest stage, already rho ~ 2.4 at c = 1, goes further over capacity as service times stretch. Second, and more importantly, the RANKING of modifications is robust: M1 and M3 remain the best on P95 at every c, and base P95 always exceeds M1 P95 across the whole sweep - the rebalance is never hurt by a slower population, it is just less dramatic in absolute terms. The accommodation recommendation follows directly: (i) the lane rebalance (M1) is the culture-robust backbone and should be the default; (ii) for populations with a slower-traveler or strong-no-cutting norm (c > 1.1), the checkpoint should additionally add Pre-Check capacity (one more Pre lane or a dedicated peak surge lane) because utilization, not traveler speed, is the binding constraint - you cannot negotiate your way out of rho > 1; (iii) to reduce the variance specifically (not just the mean), queue-discipline aids help: clearly marked single-file serpentine queues and 'lane-open' signals reduce the time a slow or hesitant passenger blocks the belt, which in the model corresponds to lowering the effective c for the divest stage without changing lane counts. In short, the system accommodates cultural differences by (a) sizing capacity to the slowest realistic traveler it must serve (design for c = 1.15-1.3 at peak), and (b) using physical queue design to keep the per-passenger service time near the calibrated median so that the speed multiplier stays close to 1.

tasks.task_description: Part (d): Propose policy and procedural recommendations for the security managers, globally applicable or tailored to specific cultures/traveler types, based on the model; and validate the model, assess its strengths and weaknesses, and propose future work.
tasks.task_analysis: The recommendations are read directly off the model's bottleneck and sensitivity results, so each is traceable to a specific finding. The validation section reports what the model was checked against (the supplied trace, the utilization algebra, the seed stability, and the parameter sweeps) and states honestly which conclusions are robust and which rest on the small-sample service-time estimates.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Recommendations, each tied to a model result: (R1, global, highest priority) Rebalance the Pre-Check to Regular lane ratio from 1:3 toward 1:1.5 (4 Pre : 6 Regular for a 10-lane checkpoint), holding total lanes and officers fixed. Model basis: this single change cuts the system P95 wait from ~223 to ~98 min and the P99 from ~240 to ~106 min with no added cost (part b, M1). (R2, global) Pool the ID-check officers into a shared queue rather than one-officer-per-lane. Model basis: trims the ID-stage idle-time variance and shaves ~10 min off the P95 on top of R1 (part b, M2/M3); cheap procedural change. (R3, peak-specific) Add one Pre-Check lane (or a surge lane opened only during the departure peak) for airports whose Pre-Check demand makes 4 Pre lanes still rho_peak > 1.5. Model basis: even the rebalanced Pre-Check divest stage runs rho_peak ~ 2.7, so a sharp peak can re-saturate it; one more lane brings it to ~1.9 and the P95 toward ~60 min (part b residual; part c). (R4, culture-tailored) For airports serving predominantly slower-traveler or strong-no-cutting populations, design capacity for a traveler-speed factor of 1.15-1.3 at peak (i.e. add Pre-Check capacity per R3) and use physical queue design - single-file serpentine lines, clearly marked bin placement, 'lane open' signage - to hold the effective per-passenger divest time near the median. Model basis: part c shows a 30%-slower population can push the base P95 to ~309 min and erode the rebalance benefit unless extra capacity is present; queue design is the lever that keeps the speed multiplier near 1 without adding lanes. (R5, global, monitoring) Instrument the checkpoint with automatic per-stage timestamps (fixed sensors at ID, belt-in, belt-out, reclaim) instead of manual time studies. Model basis: the supplied data's truncation (Exchange 1) means the current bottleneck is inferred from a small non-empty sample; continuous sensing would let the utilization rho_k be tracked live and the lane ratio (R1) retuned to the actual peak shape. The recommendation set is ordered by cost and by the size of the P95 reduction it produces: R1 (rebalance, free, largest effect) first, then R2 (shared ID, free, small effect), then R3 (extra Pre lane, capital cost, for the residual peak risk), then R4 (culture-tailored capacity + queue design, for slow-traveler populations), then R5 (instrumentation, enforces all of the above.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Validation. Strengths: (i) the model is fully reproducible from the supplied trace and three documented expert-grounded assumptions; (ii) the bottleneck identification is robust - it is driven by the demand-to-lane ratio (45% demand on 2 lanes), not by the exact service-time medians, and it survives the gamma sweep (logs/sim_sweep_gamma.log) and the 3-seed average; (iii) it reproduces the reported symptom (a heavy right tail, long unpredictable waits) rather than just the mean, which is the whole point of the variance-reduction goal; (iv) the two headline modifications are cost-free process/staffing changes that the model shows are effective (M1 cuts the system P95 wait by ~56% with no added lanes or officers). Weaknesses: (i) the trace is a single short snapshot, so the peak shape (P = 2.2, peak at 40% of the hour) and the batch-arrival probability are structural assumptions rather than fitted values, and they are the most parameter-sensitive inputs; (ii) the service-time medians are estimated from small non-empty blocks (n = 7-29 per station) and carry non-trivial uncertainty, though the bottleneck conclusion does not depend on their exact values; (iii) the model assumes one X-ray belt per lane and no cross-queue borrowing, which is the current process the problem describes but would overstate waits if a real checkpoint has additional unmodelled capacity; (iv) it reports end-to-end wait, not a per-stage breakdown, so the exact overloaded stage is identified by utilization algebra rather than by measured per-stage queues (which the truncated data cannot support). Future work: (i) fit the peak profile and the batch-arrival process to a full-day, multi-day timestamped log rather than a single snapshot; (ii) extend the model to multiple checkpoints per terminal and to the downstream effect on boarding (missed-flight cost) so the P95 criterion can be weighted by the actual cost of a missed connection; (iii) add a secondary-screening (Zone D) feedback loop, since a fraction of passengers are re-routed to additional screening, which adds a recirculation the current model does not capture; (iv) couple the DES to a live staffing optimizer that retunes the lane ratio in real time as the arrival rate is observed.
